bridge: Builds on N06 cookies, S06 sessions and W03 script boundaries. The following is a paper browser-policy fixture.
teaching:
“Automatically attached” means the browser adds an eligible cookie because of its stored cookie rules, even when a different page initiated the request. The server cannot infer the user’s intention just from that cookie.

CSRF concerns an unwanted action sent with credentials the browser attaches automatically. The attacker does not necessarily need to read the response. Therefore a cross-origin read restriction is not sufficient protection for a state-changing endpoint.

Use an anti-CSRF design appropriate to the application, such as a validated token bound to the session and checked on state changes. SameSite cookies and origin checks can add boundaries, but their exact behaviour depends on request type, browser rules and deployment. A safe method such as GET should not perform a state change merely because it is easy to link.

Same-site and same-origin are different concepts. Sibling hosts may be same-site while still cross-origin. XSS in the protected origin can often bypass CSRF assumptions because it acts within the application context. Explain the threat model of each control instead of adding flags without knowing what requests they affect.
example:
Fictional POST /change-display-name
Required: authenticated session + CSRF token equal to session's stored token
A session token for CSRF: token-A (invented)
Case1: identity A, supplied token-A -> allow
Case2: identity A, no token        -> reject
Case3: identity A, token-B         -> reject
No GET route performs the change.
explanation: The token is a separate check from authentication. A request can carry a valid session cookie but fail the anti-CSRF validation. Tokens should not be predictable or exposed in unrelated logs. This teaching value is intentionally public and must never become a real service secret.
exercise: Evaluate the three cases, then add an unauthenticated request carrying token-A and an authenticated GET attempting the same change. State expected server decisions without making network requests.
solution: Only case 1 changes state. Missing/wrong tokens reject. An unauthenticated caller cannot use the token as a login. GET must not perform the state change.
challenge: A developer says “our CORS policy prevents other sites reading responses, therefore our cookie-authenticated POST needs no CSRF protection.” Explain the missing distinction and propose two complementary checks.
challenge_solution: Preventing reads does not universally prevent sending a credentialed action. Validate a session-bound anti-CSRF token and an appropriate origin policy, with SameSite as an additional defence where suitable. Include negative state-change tests, not only response-read tests.
